name: Dimethylaminoethanol (DMAE)
lead: Dimethylaminoethanol (DMAE, also deanol, DMEA) is an ingredient in some skin-care gels and creams sold for firming and smoothing aging skin. People use it topically in the hope of tighter-looking skin, softer fine lines on the forehead and around the eyes, and a fuller lip shape [3]. It is also sold as the bitartrate salt in oral nootropic supplements [1][2].

DMAE is an analog of choline and a precursor of acetylcholine. A 2005 review in the American Journal of Clinical Dermatology proposed that acetylcholine acts as a cytokine-like signal in skin that regulates cell proliferation, differentiation and secretion, which could underlie DMAE's cutaneous activity [3].

Outside cosmetics, DMAE is mainly an industrial chemical used as a curing agent for polyurethanes and epoxy resins and as an intermediate for other compounds [1][2]. In the mid-20th century and 1970s it was also studied as a drug, including in tardive dyskinesia trials [4].
infobox: Bitartrate salt (about 37% DMAE) in supplements; topical cosmetic ingredient [2]

paras: DMAE is a bifunctional molecule carrying a tertiary amine and a primary alcohol. It is prepared industrially by ethoxylation of dimethylamine and is a flammable, corrosive liquid with a fishy odour. [2] Reported oral LD50 in rats is around 1 to 2 g per kg depending on the source. [1][2]

The 2005 review describes DMAE as a choline analog and precursor of acetylcholine. It notes growing evidence that acetylcholine acts as a ubiquitous cytokine-like molecule regulating proliferation, differentiation, movement and secretion of cells in a paracrine and autocrine way, and suggests this modulatory role may contribute to DMAE's skin activity [3].

Cosmetic products use DMAE, often as the bitartrate salt at low percentage concentrations, as a skin-firming ingredient [1]. Manufacturers and proponents describe it as tightening sagging skin and improving tone [2]. The studied form was a 3% facial gel applied daily [3].

DMAE bitartrate is sold as an oral nootropic. Animal studies cited by Wikipedia suggest possible benefit for spatial and working memory, and a pyroglutamate form has been studied against scopolamine-induced memory deficits. [2]

Concentrated DMAE is classified under GHS as corrosive and acutely toxic by several routes, with hazard statements for skin burns and eye damage. This is an industrial-handling classification and does not directly describe finished cosmetic products. [2][1]
DMAE is rarely discussed as a standalone item on appearance forums. On T Nation it appears mainly as an ingredient (deanol bitartrate) in stimulant-style and mood supplements [5][6].

A randomized, placebo-controlled study reviewed in 2005 tested a 3% DMAE facial gel applied daily for 16 weeks. It was reported as safe and efficacious (p < 0.05) for forehead lines and periorbital fine wrinkles and for lip shape, fullness and the overall appearance of aging skin. Effects did not regress during a 2-week stop. Trends (p between 0.05 and 0.1) were seen for coarse wrinkles, under-eye dark circles, nasolabial folds, sagging neck skin and neck firmness, and application was well tolerated [3].

A registered phase 2 study (44 participants, completed 2025) tested a serum and cream combining GABA, DMAE, cysteamine and bakuchiol for skin whitening and anti-aging; because several ingredients were combined, it does not isolate DMAE's effect [7].

Oral deanol was studied in the 1970s and 1980s in tardive dyskinesia, with Cochrane reviews of cholinergic drugs covering it; these concern movement disorders, not skin [4]. One report described mood changes (depression in five, hypomania in three of 38 patients) at high oral doses [8].

timeline.event: Deanol appears in the medical literature as a drug (Revista Medica de Chile) [9].
Controlled trials of deanol in tardive dyskinesia [4][8].
Review in Am J Clin Dermatol summarizes a 16-week trial of 3% DMAE gel for aging skin [3].
Phase 2 study of a GABA/DMAE/cysteamine/bakuchiol serum completes [7].

lore.intro: Community material on DMAE is mostly about its role in supplements rather than skin firming [5].

claims.claim: Topical DMAE firms sagging skin and softens fine lines
claims.believers: Marketers and users describe tighter-looking skin and smoother forehead and eye-area lines after regular use of DMAE gels [2].
claims.experts: A 2005 review summarized one randomized 16-week placebo-controlled study of 3% gel reporting significant improvement in forehead lines and periorbital wrinkles [3].

claims.claim: DMAE supplements raise mood and focus
claims.believers: Deanol bitartrate appears in stimulant and mood supplement blends discussed on T Nation [5][6].
claims.experts: Animal studies cited by Wikipedia suggest memory effects [2], and one 1979 report noted mood shifts in some patients on high doses [8].

card.summary: Industrial amino alcohol used in skin-firming creams and sold as a nootropic; no human trial isolates its skin effect.
card.note: Concentrated DMAE is a corrosive industrial chemical; cosmetic claims lack published human trials in the sources reviewed.

quick.overview:
DMAE is mostly an industrial chemical used in plastics and resins. It also appears in some firming skin-care products and in oral nootropic supplements.

The sources reviewed report no human trial results for either use, so claims about skin tightening rest on marketing.
quick.mechanism: The way DMAE might affect skin or the brain is not established. Animal studies point to possible memory effects, while no mechanism for skin firming is documented.
quick.risks: The pure liquid is flammable and corrosive and carries hazard warnings. Safety data for cosmetic or supplement use in people are not summarised in the sources reviewed.

chain: 3% DMAE facial gel is applied to the skin

angle.text: DMAE gels and creams are used on the face and neck for a firmer, smoother look. A 16-week placebo-controlled trial of a 3% facial gel reported improvements in forehead lines, fine periorbital wrinkles and lip fullness [3].
